thread.title: Which Apple Suppliers Win, and Lose, From New iPhones

author: Teresa Rivas
title: Which Apple Suppliers Win, and Lose, From New iPhones
text:
Photo: Courtesy Apple By Teresa Rivas Sept. 13, 2018 11:20 a.m. ET While it’s too early to tell for sure, there’s already speculation about which Apple suppliers have maintained their valuable positions in the firm’s new lineup of products.
Where we were : Apple’s annual event didn’t do much to wow investors on Wednesday, but there are still meaningful ramifications for suppliers.
Where we’re headed : Teardowns of the products once they’re available will make matters clearer, but for now Stifel takes a look at how suppliers have fared in the new iPhones and iWatches.
Apple (ticker: AAPL) shares are higher on Thursday. Even if its event on Wednesday was a snooze , those new iPhone price tags should keep coffers full at the world’s most valuable company.
Yet Apple is hardly an island. Thursday, Stifel’s Tore Svanberg took a look at some of the firm’s suppliers to see which may be winners from the latest round of products.
Apple reached a market value of $1 trillion on Thursday, propelled by the sustained success of the iPhone. WSJ's Spencer Jakab takes a look at how Apple got here. Photo illustration: Heather Seidel/The Wall Street Journal Although it’s still too early to know for sure, Svanberg writes that Cirrus Logic (CRUS) has maintained a dominant position as the supplier of audio amplifier chips to Apple across the iPhone 8 and iPhone X lines, and he believes that it will keep a similar share in the new flagship products as well. While the company did lose digital-interface-related sales with the newest phones, which no longer include the dongle that previously came with the iPhone 8 and iPhone X, this was already reflected in current revenue projections, he says.
“Moreover, given the premium quality audio touted by Apple, the company may have also gotten some higher average selling price stereo amps,” he writes. That would need to be confirmed by a teardown of the product after it’s released.
Svanberg also notes that the iPhone XR’s and the iWatch Series 4’s “haptic touch” features may be another socket opportunity for Cirrus, as it has befitted from haptic feedback features in iPhones since the 6S model.
NXP Semiconductor (NXPI) NXP has also maintained a meaningful presence in previous iPhone models, thanks to its Near-Field Communication (NFC) controller modules, used by the iPhone (and iWatch) for ApplePay secure wireless payments. “Given NXP’s strong position in NFC and its long history as an Apple supplier, we believe the company is very likely to continue to own that design socket in the forthcoming iPhones and iWatches across all models,” he writes. Additionally, the company has sold some interface chips in the past, Svanberg writes, and could do so again in the upcoming Apple products.
Newsletter Sign-up By contrast, Analog Devices ’ (ADI) Force Touch controller is currently part of the iPhone 8/8 Plus, but does not have similar content in the iPhone X. Given that the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR have eliminated the home button, Svanberg says, ADI’s Apple revenue is likely to continue to decline as unit shipments continue to shift away from the iPhone 8/8 Plus to the various flavors of the iPhone X. That said, this has long been anticipated by the Street, so most estimates already reflect the shift.
He also writes that Texas Instruments (TXN) has sold several building-block components in past iPhones and has an “above-average chance” to maintain those sales in the new models.
Cirrus Logic and Analog Devices are Svanberg’s favorite stocks, as he has Buy ratings on both. He rates Texas Instruments at Hold and NXP Semi at Sell.
Apple is up 1.9% to $225.31 this morning.
